title: Hourly to Annual Salary: How to Calculate Your Pay, Tax, Super, and Salary Continuance Cover
description: Convert hourly to annual salary with our calculator. Learn about National Minimum Wage, award rates, casual loading, super, tax, and salary continuance cover for Australian workers
salarySummary: Assuming a 38-hour week, an hourly rate of $26.44 (the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026) gives an annual gross salary of $52,254.40 before tax and super.

faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then multiply by 52. For a standard full-time week of 38 hours, the formula is hourly × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual pay before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and an award rate?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage ($26.44/hr from 1 July 2026) applies to employees not covered by an award. Most employees are covered by a modern award that sets higher minimum rates for their industry or occupation. Award rates also include penalty rates, allowances, and overtime provisions.

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated on my hourly pay?
faqs.a: Super is paid by your employer on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (from 1 July 2026) up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. It is not deducted from your hourly rate. For example, if your annual gross is $52,254.40, your employer contributes an extra $6,270.53 to your super fund.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Your Hourly Rate to Annual Salary

When you receive an hourly rate offer or are comparing a salary, the first step is to understand the annual equivalent. The standard formula used across Australia is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**

This calculation assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. For most full-time employees, the standard week is 38 hours, as set by the National Employment Standards (NES) under the Fair Work Act. If you are part-time or casual, your weekly hours may vary, and you should use your actual average hours.

For example, the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour. For a 38-hour week, that equals $1,004.90 per week ($26.44 × 38) and $52,254.40 per year ($1,004.90 × 52). This is the minimum an award-free employee aged 21 or over can be paid. However, most employees are covered by a modern award or enterprise agreement that sets higher minimum rates.

### The Fortnightly Pay Period

Many employers pay fortnightly. Your fortnightly gross pay is simply your weekly pay multiplied by two. Using the minimum wage example, that would be $2,009.80 before tax. Knowing your fortnightly amount helps with budgeting and comparing salary offers that are quoted per annum.

## National Minimum Wage vs. Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage applies to employees not covered by an award or agreement. It is reviewed annually by the Fair Work Commission. As of 1 July 2026, the rate is $26.44 per hour for full-time and part-time employees, and $33.05 per hour for casual employees (including the 25% casual loading). This is confirmed by the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay guides.

However, the vast majority of Australian employees work under a modern award. Awards set minimum pay rates for specific industries and occupations, and these rates are often higher than the National Minimum Wage. For example, the Supported Employment Services Award (MA000103) has its own pay guide with rates effective from 30 June 2026 and 1 July 2026. To find the correct award for your job, use the Fair Work Ombudsman's Pay and Conditions Tool.

### Casual Loading

Casual employees are entitled to a loading of at least 25% on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave (annual leave, sick leave). This loading is included in the casual minimum wage of $33.05 per hour. When using our calculator, you can check the "casual loading" box to add 25% to your base rate. Do not enter a rate that already includes casual loading; the calculator will add it for you.

## Superannuation Guarantee

Superannuation is paid by your employer on top of your ordinary earnings. From 1 July 2026, the Super Guarantee rate is 12% of ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. This means if your annual gross salary is $52,254.40, your employer must contribute an additional $6,270.53 into your super fund (12% of $52,254.40). Super is not deducted from your pay; it is an extra cost to the employer. However, it is part of your total remuneration package.

When comparing a salary offer to an hourly rate, remember that salary often includes super in the quoted figure, whereas hourly rates are typically quoted exclusive of super. Always check whether the figure is "base salary" or "total package including super." Our calculator shows super as an estimated amount paid on top.

## Tax and Take-Home Pay

Your annual gross pay is subject to income tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income over $190,000

Additionally, the Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. Our calculator uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds for Medicare as the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of calculation. Note that this is an estimate; your actual tax may vary based on your circumstances, including the Medicare levy surcharge, HELP repayments, or salary packaging.

For a full-time worker on the National Minimum Wage ($52,254.40), the estimated tax would be approximately $7,717 (using the 2026–27 rates) plus Medicare levy of $1,045, giving a total of $8,762, leaving a take-home pay of about $43,492 per year. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page for more detailed estimates.

## Salary Continuance Cover: An Important Consideration

When evaluating your total compensation, don't overlook benefits such as **salary continuance cover**. This is an insurance policy that replaces a portion of your income if you are unable to work due to illness or injury. Some employers offer it as part of a salary package, especially for permanent employees. While it is not directly related to hourly-to-annual conversion, it affects the overall value of your employment. A salary with salary continuance cover may be more attractive than a higher hourly rate without it, because it provides financial protection. Always ask about such benefits when negotiating a job offer.

## Using Our Calculator

Our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool allows you to enter your base hourly rate and optionally add casual loading. It then calculates your annual, weekly, and fortnightly gross pay, estimated tax, Medicare levy, and superannuation. The results assume a 38-hour week unless you specify otherwise. Remember that this is an estimate; your actual pay and conditions are determined by your award, enterprise agreement, or contract.

For more information on minimum wages, award pay guides, and entitlements, visit the Fair Work Ombudsman website. They provide the most authoritative and up-to-date information.

## Summary

Converting your hourly rate to an annual salary is straightforward: multiply by hours per week and 52 weeks. But the real picture includes award rates, casual loading, super, tax, and benefits like salary continuance cover. Always check the applicable award or agreement for your exact entitlements. Our calculator gives you a quick estimate to compare offers and plan your finances.
